Question: I see some C programmers switching to C++ but still coding in C style or not fully using C++? Are the two programming paradigms too difficult to switch?
Answer: There are some huge differences between procedural programming and object-oriented programming. The biggest one is the idea of runtime polymorphism, supported by virtual member functions in C++. C has no direct equivalent. It has the net effect of turning your call stack upside down. Instead of one function calling another function, we have something calling … we don’t know what exactly. The benefit of this is that we can design a system that can call any compatible function, not just a single one. This allows us to get rid of a lot of conditional statements. It also allows us to write code that can have new functionality added, without changing the existing code. All of that is possible in C (using struct and function pointers). But it does not have that direct support in the C language itself, so it is perhaps less often used. That’s the learning curve going from procedural C to object-oriented C++.

Question: What is the main work of a software engineer, and how can I be an expert in software engineering?
Answer: Where I find myself with this is that a software engineer: Gaining expertise is like anything else. It takes time. You have to understand what it is that you are doing, why you are doing it and why you are not doing some alternative. You slowly build knowledge from a variety of sources. This knowledge is turned into wisdom by applying it to real problems. As you do so, you find new insights into that knowledge. You find areas where it does not work out as you thought it might. You find connections between different areas of the subject, that spark new approaches. The starting point with code is learning how to write small programs - small meaning between 1 and 50 lines of code - that do simple things. They will use the fundamental concepts of programming, like variables, conditional branching, loops. Explore simple data structures like arrays, lists and maps. Work with simple algorithms, like finding the total of an array of numbers. Later on, it becomes important to learn how to organise software. How to decompose a big problem into largely separate smaller sub problems. How to specify, design and test software components. How to work with the web, databases, user interfaces and more. But you can only start at the beginning. Learn. Apply. Reflect. improve. And then keep going.

Question: What’s the best way to grasp object oriented programming?
Answer: (from my book Java OOP Done Right) I think of all the objects as little people at work, each one having a job to do. Each one knows how to do their job, and has all the reference books and supplies they need to do it. So we might have a writer, who writes a letter. This letter is then handed to a postman. The postman drives the letter to a sorting office. The sorting office has inside it a big map of postcodes, and on that map each postcode has a little pin with the name of another postman, who is responsible for delivering the letters. The sorting office hands over the letter to the correct postman, who delivers it to a reader. The writer does not tell the postman how to deliver the letter. Nor does the writer ask the postman anything at all about how the delivery will be done. Each person does their own job, without interference. This is the essence of OOP. I have just described encapsulation - which is the sorting office having a map of postcodes and postmen. Nobody else needs to see that map - it is private data. I’ve also described object messaging. The writer object sends a ‘post this’ message to the postman object. This is also object collaboration. I’ve described the single responsibility principle. Each object does it’s own part of the job. But just that piece; the writer object does not attempt to help the postman. They split up jobs. In code, you might have something like this: And then a process would happen: sorting office looks up the right delivery postman for the postcode W12 8QT, and calls: This is very roughly the essence of OOP. You split a complex job up into small, self contained pieces. And I think of it as little people, who have enough private knowledge to do a small job very well. The big job is done by having many of these little people work together to do their parts. I’ve turned this into a book at Java OOP Done Right which covers how I like to get the best out of OOP in Java, using SOLID principles, TDD and more. Basically, all the stuff I use everyday to create clean, high quality OOP code.

Question: Why do private and methods variables exist in OOP? Couldn't you just avoid using code that would access the variables?
Answer: You get private in many languages even non OOP ones. Marking something as private does a few things: I got sold on this idea when at work in an embedded software job. The change was to make the display flash more quickly for a certain kind of error. The change was made. The result was a quicker flash AND losing all the stored configuration data of the machine. Oops. This happened because a global variable had been used as the flash timer. A different change then used that same variable to control the data write timing. At the time, it was a perfect match in timing. Speeding up the display - and so the write timing - violated the maximum write speed. It took ages to track that down. None of the code appeared to be wrong. Nobody thought they had even touched the config storage code. This should never have happened. Those two disparate features should never have been coupled together. But the variable was not private. So it was possible to couple them. Without the full context of knowing the whole system, it was a mistake waiting to happen. Using a private flash timer fully encapsulated in the display module would have prevented this, and made the code more clear to a human reader.

Question: They say choose C# over Java if you are a Windows user, but what does this have to do with the fact that my goal is web development and not desktop apps?
Answer: “They” is your problem here. Never uncritically listen to “them”. Choose advisors wisely. You can develop server-side web apps in almost anything. Choose from Java, C#, Go, Python, JavaScript, Typescript, Rust, Haskell … and a hundred other languages. All you need really is a general purpose language you like, the ability to communicate HTTP commands over TCP sockets and a templating language to render either JSON or HTML. Done and done. The advantage of Windows .NET when you start out is that it is one thing. You open the box and turn the key. You’re off. Java, by comparison, is a little more pick and mix. You get many choices that all simply get in the way when you’re starting. They make very little difference to the end result, but still require decisions to be made. Go is pretty good as it has everything you need built in. But so does C# and Java if you pair it with (eg) vtence.molecule. Most modern web apps use a mix of server-side “heavy lifting” - application logic, business rules, storage - and client-side view rendering. On the client, we will often choose a UI framework like React (or angular, vue … or many others). This taks lumps of JSON data (usually) and converts that for display inside the browser. That will call for a bit of knowledge about html and CSS. So the direct answer to your question is “nothing”. Choosing C# would not impede your ability to make web apps. It’s not your only choice.

Question: Is the assertion of Brooks's Law, "adding manpower to a late software project makes it later," still considered accurate, or has it been deemed an exaggeration? If the principle is still valid, what are the reasons behind its continued applicability?
Answer: Yes. The principle behind it is our inability to predict the future well, combined with our difficulty communicating relevant information Splitting work across a team means making interface contracts that perfectly isolate each work piece. We need to understand the work we need to do in detail. Generally we discover this later as we build for real. The hidden difficulties we never foresaw emerge later, as the unknown unknowns become visible. As people increase, we get too many divisions such that we can not achieve clean splits. Then we trip over each other. To compound the problem, many people assume developing software is manufacturing. Make one widget, hire ten staff, make ten identical widgets. It is not, has never and will never be like this. That independence and repeatability of components and assembly is not there. If you fix these issues, Brooks Law will disappear. You will be the first to do so.

Question: Can an expert programmer understand everything when they look into any source code of any program without the documentation?
Answer: Nuanced answer: no but yes. Source code is the most accurate documentation of what problem is being solved and how. That is what source code is. It’s for human consumption. The stuff the computer executes is object code, which is a wholly different thing, So yes - you can understand everything by looking at the source code. That is precisely how the compiler (or interpreter) understand what the object code must do. Source code includes the suite of automated tests, deployment scripts, and data schema migrations. Tests like these are (or should be) executable specifications of behaviour and intended usage patterns. The other infrastructure as code components explain how the hardware is to be set up and how data is organised. There should be a lot of explanatory information in source code. But … humans. It is easier to write source code that only the compiler understands than it is to write for humans. So no - sometimes the damn code doesn’t seem to mean a thing. And our industry is happy with programmers who write like that.

Question: Why are uncaught exceptions thrown by a unit test?
Answer: Uncaught exceptions always bubble up to the top of the running thread. But that’s not the important thing here. Your test - presumably - should pass. It either should assert that the exception was thrown (because that’s what the code should be doing). Or the code should not be throwing an exception. Check the arrange step for how the code is wired up. Check how it is being run in the act step. Debug which statement is throwing and why. The test is telling you that the code does not and cannot work under the test conditions set. If the test used to pass, you just broke the code in the last change. Revert, understand, have another go. If it’s a new test, you haven’t got the code right yet.
